newsitem.title: RUSSIA: U.S. defence chief clashes with Duma on arms pact.
newsitem.headline: U.S. defence chief clashes with Duma on arms pact.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry fenced with hostile Russian legislators in a hard-nosed exchange on nuclear arms cuts on Thursday, apparently doing little to reverse overwhelming opposition to the START-2 treaty.
Perry pressed members of the State Duma, parliament's lower house, to ratify the strategic arms reduction treaty which would slash U.S. and Russian warheads to about 3,000 on each side by 2003.

But U.S. and Russian officials said afterwards that START-2, ratified by the U.S. Senate this year, remained in deep trouble mainly because of deep Russian suspicions of planned NATO expansion into eastern Europe.

"Ratification of START-2 is quite problematic, it is not in the interest of the Russian side," Duma defence committee chairman Lev Rokhlin told Perry, who testified that each nation could save nearly $5 billion over five years by destroying warheads instead of maintaining huge arsenals.

"Russians are disappointed with tendencies emerging in America, and it would be difficult to convince the Russian public that the United States is friendly and has peaceful intentions towards Russia," Vladimir Lukin, chairman of the Duma's international committee, said after the meeting.

Perry told reporters later at a news conference that he had no way of assessing whether he had changed any minds, but said he had made clear to the Duma that planned NATO enlargement would not be abandoned in order to get START-2 approved.
"I was not there to discuss trade-offs between other factors," he said.
Pentagon spokesman Ken Bacon told reporters there was a lot of suspicion in the Duma. "This is going to be an uphill fight. There is no doubt about it," he said.

Perry said he was pleased to present the U.S. case on Start-2 and that he told the Duma that the United States was willing to start talks immediately on a START-3 nuclear reduction treaty immediately after START-2 was passed.
START-2 would cut U.S. and Russian strategic nuclear arsenals to about 3,000 warheads from current levels of over 6,000 each. That would be a third of Cold War levels.
A number of Russian legislators, including communist leader Gennady Zyuganov, voiced continuing suspicion of START-2 and repeated fierce opposition to NATO expansion.
The Russian economy and its military forces are in disarray and many Russian officials fear that cutting nuclear weapons deeply would leave Moscow open to blackmail from the West.
"I believe the START-2 treaty is fair and gives neither side an advantage," Perry told Duma members in a speech before he was bombarded by hostile questions on U.S.-Russian relations and NATO.
He said the warheads remaining under START-2 would be "enough to destroy the world" and "more than enough deterrence" for Russia.

The treaty would eliminate Russia's big multiple-warhead SS-18 intercontinental missiles and leave each country with only single-warhead land-based missiles and multiple-warhead missiles based aboard submarines.
Perry tried to brush aside suspicion by some questioners that the United States might develop new and better single-warhead land-based intercontinental missiles if the treaty was ratified.
"Both of us know that fewer nuclear weapons in the world makes us all safer." he added. "Why would we want more missiles? We already have more warheads and missiles than we need."

Republican U.S. Senator Richard Lugar of Indiana and Democratic Senator Joseph Lieberman of Connecticut said the questioning was harsh and showed deep suspicion of U.S. motives after the Cold War, but they said that the government of President Boris Yeltsin supported START-2.
Both senators voiced confidence that government influence would eventually prevail on the Duma.
